note.note:
History:
- Presenting complaint: 5-day history of cough and constant nasal discharge.
- Cough: dry, occurs approximately every 20–30 minutes, non-productive, no blood.
- Nasal symptoms: constant streaming, green discharge, no epistaxis.
- Systemic symptoms: subjective fevers (feels hot at times) with intermittent chills; no thermometer reading documented.
- Gastrointestinal: brief diarrhoea around the time of onset that has since resolved; no current vomiting or diarrhoea.
- Other symptoms: myalgias (achy muscles); no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no pleuritic pain, no rash, no headache, no visual change, no sore throat reported.
- Course/progression and context: symptoms began ~5 days ago; patient self-treated with lemon-based hot drinks (Lemsip/lemon sips) 2–3 times daily with some symptomatic relief, especially at night. Patient reports being generally well otherwise.

Past Medical History:
- Chronic illnesses: diabetes (type not specified) and hypertension.
- Medications: metformin — dose/route/frequency not documented; lisinopril — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient stated “two hundred” when asked about dose; dose unclear/conflict noted).
- Allergies: seasonal hay fever (allergic rhinitis) intermittently; no known medication allergies reported.

Physical Examination:
- No formal physical examination findings documented in the transcript.
- Patient-reported/observed negatives: no throat swelling reported, alert and conversational, no respiratory distress, no hemoptysis, able to eat/drink and pass urine normally.
- Reported signs: subjective feeling of being hot; nasal green discharge.

Impression:
- Probable upper respiratory tract infection with chest symptoms consistent with a likely viral chest infection; patient with diabetes may have increased risk of secondary bacterial infection.

Management Plan:
- Immediate/advised actions:
  - Obtain and record an oral/tympanic thermometer reading (thermometer can be purchased at a pharmacy).
  - Continue supportive measures (hot lemon/Lemsip). Do not take additional paracetamol-containing products concurrently with Lemsip.
  - Use cough syrup only at night if cough prevents sleep; avoid daytime cough suppression if not required.
- Safety-netting / when to re-contact:
  - Reassess/seek medical advice if temperature remains persistently elevated (doctor referenced >37.5–38°C), if fevers continue/spike, if cough worsens or becomes productive with purulent sputum, if coughs up blood, develops new nosebleeds, shortness of breath, or chest pain.
  - If symptoms meet above criteria, antibiotics may be considered at re-evaluation given diabetes.
- Chronic care advice:
  - Continue regular diabetes and blood-pressure monitoring as per GP recommendations.

Patient Summary:
- Patient with diabetes and hypertension developed a 5-day history of dry cough and green nasal discharge with subjective fevers and myalgias. Symptoms are most consistent with a viral upper respiratory/chest infection. Plan is symptomatic treatment, to obtain a thermometer and monitor temperature, and to contact clinician/GP if fever persists, symptoms worsen or new red-flag symptoms develop (then consider antibiotics).

Key Takeaways:
- Buy and use a thermometer to check and record temperature.
- Continue Lemsip/lemon drinks but avoid additional paracetamol-containing products concurrently.
- Return promptly if fever persists/spikes, cough worsens or becomes productive, or if shortness of breath/chest pain/hemoptysis develops.

Next Steps:
- Patient to obtain thermometer and monitor temperature regularly.
- Re-contact clinician/GP for review if fever persists (>37.5–38°C) or if respiratory symptoms worsen; possible antibiotic consideration if bacterial infection suspected.
- Ensure routine follow-up with GP for ongoing diabetes and blood-pressure management.

  - No physical examination documented (respiratory auscultation, throat/nasal exam).

  - Smoking status not documented.
